notes.meaning: This record names the five sons of Shobal, who was the second son of Seir the Horite. These Horites were the original cave-dwelling people living in the hills of Seir before Esau's family grew large. The family trees are preserved to show the tribes that lived alongside and eventually blended into Edom.

Zibeon had two sons, Aiah and Anah. While Anah was out caring for his father's donkeys in the dry wilderness, he discovered hot springs of water. Faithful care in ordinary, daily chores often leads to unexpected help and blessings.

Anah had a son named Dishon and a daughter named Oholibamah. This daughter shares the same name as one of Esau's wives, showing how closely Esau's household connected with the native Horite families. It reminds us that marriage ties quickly brought different peoples together in the ancient world.

These four men were the sons of Dishon, who was another son of Seir. Each of these sons grew into a family group in the mountains. God keeps track of all human families, even those outside the covenant line of Abraham.

Ezer was another son of Seir, and these three men were his sons. They helped make up the network of Horite clans in the land. Even short lists of names show how faithfully God watched over the growth of nations.

Dishan was the seventh son of Seir, and he had two sons named Uz and Aran. The name Uz later became attached to the desert region where Job lived. These family lines helped shape the map of the ancient desert world.

These verses sum up the seven main clan leaders of the Horites in the land of Seir. These chiefs were not single rulers of a whole nation; they led their own separate families at the same time. In time, Esau's family would conquer and absorb these older tribes.

Edom began setting up kings long before Israel had any earthly king of its own. God had promised Jacob that kings would come from his descendants, but Esau's family reached worldly power much sooner. Earthly success often comes quickly to the world, while God's people must wait patiently for His promises.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this note as a comment added during the time of Israel's kings, looking back to compare Israel's monarchy with Edom's earlier rulers.

notes.meaning: Bela son of Beor was the first recorded king in Edom, ruling from his city named Dinhabah. Nothing else is known about his life or deeds. His reign marks the beginning of Edom's shift from separate tribal chiefs to a unified king.

After Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from the city of Bozrah became king. Bozrah was an important fortified town in Edom that the later prophets often mentioned. Bela's son did not inherit the throne, showing that kings were chosen from different places rather than passing rule from father to son.

When Jobab died, Husham from the southern district of Teman took the throne. The region of Teman was famous in the ancient world for its trade and wisdom. This king shows that power continued to shift among the different districts of Edom.

Hadad son of Bedad became the next king, and his home city was Avith. He won a major battle against the Midianites in the fields of Moab. This ancient military victory was remembered in Edom's royal history for generations.

When Hadad died, Samlah from the town of Masrekah ruled in his place. Like the rulers before him, he came from a different town and family. Worldly kingdoms change hands often, but God's covenant kingdom remains steady.

Samlah was followed on the throne by Shaul, who came from Rehoboth on the river. If this refers to the Euphrates River, it means a ruler from far away was invited or fought his way to power in Edom. It reminds us that kingship in Edom was not fixed to one royal family.

Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king after Shaul died. His name points to the false god Baal, showing the pagan religious influences around Edom. The nation flourished politically while drifting away from the true God of Isaac.

Hadad ruled after Baal-hanan from the city of Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel. Unlike all the kings before him, the text does not say he died. This strongly suggests he was the king still ruling Edom when this list was first put together.

These verses name six of the later chiefs of Esau: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, and Pinon. This list is organized by regions and settled territories rather than just family birth order. Over time, the names of these clan leaders became the names of the districts and towns they ruled.

The list concludes with chiefs Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram, ruling their settled lands in Mount Seir. The chapter closes by reminding us that Esau is the father of the whole Edomite nation. While Israel was still waiting without a homeland, Esau's family already had full possession of their own country.
